newsitem.title: USA: Orange juice prices fall, USDA shows no crop damage.
newsitem.headline: Orange juice prices fall, USDA shows no crop damage.

text.p: Frozen concentrated orange juice prices fell sharply Wednesday after the Agriculture Department reported Florida's orange crop survived a winter freeze in good shape.
Soybean and rice prices bounded higher after the Agriculture Department reported smaller-than-expected stocks of both before this year's harvests.
The Agriculture Department surprised traders by raising the yield of this year's Florida orange crop, while traders expected a decrease because of a Jan. 19 freeze.
The Agriculture Department kept the crop unchanged at 220 million 90-pound boxes and raised yields to 1.54 gallons per box from 1.53 gallons.

According to the Agriculture Department, "temperatures were not low enough, long enough to cause serious damage to citrus trees." Harvesting accelerated on the early fruit with most of the damaged crops going to the processors, it said.
Also, some analysts said the Agriculture Department probably underestimated the crop in its initial report and would have raised the box count without the freeze.
At the New York Cotton Exchange, March frozen concentrated orange juice closed down 5.35 cents to 74.55 cents a pound after earlier falling to a contract low of 72.50 cents.

Soybeans at the Chicago Board of Trade had double-digit gains and the March contract touched a four-month high after the Agriculture Department reduced by 15 million bushels its year-end stocks estimate.

The Agriculture Department raised its soybean export and processing estimates, which should lower stocks to 140 million bushels before the 1997 harvest this fall. Analysts and traders had expected a cut but had speculated the Agriculture Department would be more conservative.
"It's a somewhat friendly report paced by the soy complex with the carryout cut to 140 million bushels," said Robert Lekberg, grain analyst for Chicago-based trade house Goldenberg, Hehmeyer and Co.

The increases in U.S. soybean usage offset the Agriculture Department's larger crop estimates for Brazil and Argentina. Brazil was expected to harvest 26.50 million metric tons, up 0.05 million from the previous report and Argentina 13.50 million, up 0.5 million.
March soybeans closed up 14-1/2 cents at $7.64-1/4 per bushel after peaking at $7.65-1/2 per bushel, the highest since Oct. 2 when that contract touched $7.75.
CBOT rough rice futures were sharply higher for the second day after the Agriculture Department slashed 1 million hundredweight from its estimate of supplies remaining before harvest in August.
"This is a supply driven market," said Neauman Coleman, Dean Witter analyst, of the rice market.

Agriculture Department Wednesday lowered its U.S. ending rice stocks estimate to 24.3 million hundredweight from 25.3 million in January. It raised export projections to 75.0 million hundredweight from 74.0 million.
CBOT rice closed higher, with March up 29 cents at $12.155 per hundred pounds.

Crude oil, heating oil and gasoline futures closed lower pressured by profit-taking after early gains. A bullish American Petroleum Institute stocks report fuelled early buying, but that weakened late.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, March crude oil ended off 56 cents a barrel at $21.86. March heating oil was 1.01 cents lower at 60.85 cents per gallon, and March gasoline ended off 1.07 cents at 62.89 cents per gallon.
